title: US Outposts Were Dangerous Bubbles: How the War on Terror Trapped Itself
dek: US outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages, but became magnets for conflict. The harder they fought, the heavier they became, losing mobility, until they were trapped by the fortresses they built.
why: Wesley Morgan served in Afghanistan and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the War on Terror: tactical success alongside strategic failure. Worth pondering for anyone concerned with war and organizations.
who: Readers interested in military history, US tactics, and organizational behavior, especially those curious about the inside story of the War on Terror and military decision-making.

points.h: The outpost became a dangerous bubble
points.body: In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan embedded with troops in Afghanistan's Pech Valley and found that US outposts, meant to provide security for villages, actually became ‘dangerous bubbles’ that drew conflict toward the villagers. Both US forces and the enemy suffered few casualties; it was the villages outside the outposts that truly suffered. This contrast led him to ask: who built these outposts, why, and when—ultimately resulting in his book The Hardest Place.

points.h: The US military grew heavier and clumsier
points.body: From 2006 to 2010, US forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, tethered to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006, the 10th Mountain Division could still use pickup trucks and ATVs to reach remote areas, but by 2010, due to the IED threat and top-down force protection requirements, conventional forces could barely reach those places, relying on special forces for offensive operations. This overextension meant subsequent units could not sustain the earlier range of activity.

points.h: Two ODA teams: restraint versus recklessness
points.body: In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, adopted an ‘inkblot’ strategy, trying to establish security around the district center and refusing to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something was luring them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to enter the Korengal to find a fight, only to get entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, used as muscle for one faction, starting the Korengal ‘snowball’ that eventually became a fierce battlefield lasting years.

points.h: Three incompatible tribes within the US military
points.body: In eastern Afghanistan, three ‘tribes’ existed within the US military: conventional forces, Green Berets (working with local partners such as training Afghan National Army commandos and local police), and the Joint Special Operations Task Force (such as Task Force 373, composed mainly of SEAL Team 6 and Rangers, conducting night raids). These three had different objectives, sometimes supporting each other but more often hindering each other. For example, the task force might kill someone conventional forces could have easily arrested, while only the task force could operate in remote areas beyond the reach of conventional forces. This lack of coordination was a core problem of the Afghanistan war.

points.h: Commanders measured success with the wrong metrics
points.body: Many commanders lacked true understanding in counterinsurgency and could only rely on quantifiable performance metrics such as ordnance dropped, miles of road built, and number of meetings held. The book gives an example: the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, during 15 months of combat in Kunar Province, lost 24 soldiers. Its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent, and 10,000 Beanie Babies distributed—metrics that could not reflect actual effects and were even self-contradictory.

Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior US Navy and Air Force officers have a chapter in their careers completely different from the conventional path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Afghanistan's Kunar and Nuristan provinces, including submarine officers, nuclear engineers, and naval aviators. For example, current INDOPACOM commander Sam Paparo led the Nuristan PRT for a year. These assignments coincided with the fighting in Wana and Narisan, and they went out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. This experience became a unique mark on their careers.

points.h: Military-media relations went from transparent to hostile
points.body: Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which units to embed with, and public affairs just helped him reach company and platoon level. But today, since the embed system ended in 2013-2014, military-media relations have deteriorated sharply, with a new generation of officers at battalion level and below viewing the media as something terrifying. He believes the turning point was not the McChrystal affair, but after Obama's second term, when the military began restricting embeds, keeping the war out of sight, because the complex message that ‘advisors’ were actually ‘combat advisors’ was unwelcome.

points.h: How Multicam became a mark of elite status
points.body: Morgan tells the story of Multicam's spread: it was invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art school graduate, lost the Army's camo competition (the Army chose the poorly performing ACU), but Delta Force adopted Multicam privately because ACU performed badly at night. It then spread through special forces, becoming a mark of elite status. Crucially, Crye hinted to game producers that this was elite camo, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before real photos, building an elite image in the minds of young soldiers.
